sections.title: Decision Summary
sections.requirement_single: Introduce the cinema itself, in developed natural paragraphs: the room and its proportions, its intended use where the interpretation states one, the display and why it suits the room, the seating arrangement, the system architecture, the most important design considerations, and the experience this design is intended to deliver. Write as an experienced cinema designer would write for a homeowner or architect. Do not list equipment, do not dump specifications, and do not restate the performance claim here. Never say this proposal outlines, this design presents, this option, decision or selected option. Where the project has real design substance, develop this in three or four paragraphs: the room and the scale of the experience, then the system and how it relates to the room, then the reasoning that makes this specification right for this project, then the result. Roughly 180 to 250 words at that depth, less where the design is genuinely simple, and never padded with invented detail to reach a length. This is the one section that establishes the whole cinema, so it takes the design's own story rather than the top-scoring result. Explain the reasoning the design_philosophy block records: what the client wants to achieve, which listening positions are prioritised, how the display and the seating were balanced, the practical constraints, the coverage and bass approaches, and why the finished design suits this brief. Never invent a reason, a priority, a budget or a decision the interpretation does not record, and never present the highest available level as the objective regardless of cost or practical consequence.
sections.requirement: State the decision between the options in the pack's own framing, and only where the pack allows a framing.

sections.title: What Stays the Same
sections.requirement: State only what every option shares, from the shared-result claims the pack allows. Where the copy also contrasts the options, cite the shared-result claims for what is unchanged and the pack's factual-change or material-gain claims for what differs.
sections.requirement_single: Explain how the system is arranged, in terms of what the client hears from each part: the loudspeaker layout, where the screen channels, the surrounds and any overhead loudspeakers the design actually has are placed, the seating and the display, and how those parts work together in this room. Describe the layout this design HAS: never state a channel count, never name a layer, a format or a loudspeaker the design does not include, and never explain how a mechanism works or why a measurement matters. Write from the design-identity and shared-result claims the pack allows, and from the interpretation's account of the architecture. Never mention another option or a baseline.

sections.title: What Changes
sections.requirement: State only the differences the pack records, and call one a gain only where the pack allows a gain.
sections.requirement_single: Explain why this solution suits this project: the choices that were made, such as the loudspeaker family, the layout and the bass approach, and what each one gives the client in this room. Write from the ranked strength stories and the credibility claims the pack allows, and from the design decisions and constraints the interpretation states. Never state or imply a comparison with another option or a baseline, and never write filler such as "there are no changes to report". This is the judgement section of the document: explain why this solution suits this particular room, how the competing priorities were balanced, which decisions carry the most value, why a compromise is reasonable where the interpretation records one, and what the client gains from the finished design. Where the design already takes an improvement without substantial additional expenditure, say what it gives the client; where an opportunity remains a design choice, say nothing about it.

sections.title: Key Performance Highlights
sections.requirement_single: State what engineering evidence supports this proposal: the recorded results the pack's claims carry, for the areas that carry a claim, in a small number of concise benefit-led sentences. Use the strength ranking to choose what is stated here, never to fix the order of the document. No dBC values, Hz values, angles, channel counts or grades: the proof belongs in the specialist sections. Never copy a complete evidence statement. No overall-seat equality claim.
sections.requirement: State the pack's recorded results, in the pack's own words, for the areas that carry a claim.

sections.title: Spatial Resolution
sections.requirement_single: Open on the listening experience itself: sound placed precisely where the action is, so an effect comes from the point on screen it belongs to; movement between loudspeakers that sounds natural and continuous rather than handed from one speaker to the next; a soundfield that extends beyond the picture into the room and reaches around and above the audience; and an immersion that holds as a scene builds. Then explain how this design's loudspeaker arrangement produces those benefits: where the screen, surround, front-wide and overhead loudspeakers sit, how the seating relates to them, and what that placement is doing for the listener. Never open by confirming that positions fall within a recommended limit or a placement zone, and never let the section read as a compliance or placement check: state the arrangement as the reason the experience works. Keep this section to speaker placement and what it does for the listener: never state a viewing angle, screen size or viewing distance here, because the picture and seating belong to the design description, and use a result only where it strengthens the point rather than listing quantities, angles or levels. Where level consistency is mentioned, say what the evidence shows (for example, front-channel levels held closely across the listed seats) instead of rating it with a word such as excellent. Stay within the claims the pack allows.
sections.requirement: Explain what the spatial results mean for the seating, within the claims the pack allows.

sections.title: Dynamic Range
sections.requirement_single: Explain both ends of dynamic range and why the contrast between them matters. The quiet end: subtle atmosphere, fine detail, delicate musical passages and dialogue that stay clear and intelligible without being pushed. The loud end: sudden impact, dynamic peaks, and the scale and physical presence of demanding soundtrack moments. The contrast is the point: a system that resolves low-level detail and then delivers real impact is what carries a soundtrack's emotional range, so explain what each end gives the listener in this room and why moving between them is what makes the moment land. Write it in three natural paragraphs: clarity at everyday listening levels, the output reserve the screen channels and surrounds hold for demanding peaks, and the physical impact the subwoofer adds. Draw each point from the saved P12, P13 and P14 evidence and say what that evidence means for the listener (for example, that the reserve lets peaks arrive without strain), rather than quoting levels; use a figure only where it makes the meaning clearer. Output capability says nothing about how quietly detail is resolved, so the quiet end rests on the design and the evidence that actually supports it. CAPABILITY IS NOT HEADROOM: for the screen channels (Parameter 12) and the surrounds and overheads (Parameter 13), describe the output capability the saved result supports and never claim an output reserve, margin or headroom unless a headroom figure is stated in the capability evidence of that claim. Where only a limiting speaker group or a level is stated, say the channels are capable for the demanding moments and stop. Only Parameter 14 states a quantified margin: where its capability evidence gives an achieved capability, a selected target and a headroom figure, say plainly that the predicted bass capability sits above the selected target by that amount (for example, predicted bass capability of 114.2 dBC against the selected 109 dBC target, a margin of 5.22 dB). Present it as a margin over the selected target only: never say it reaches a higher RP22 performance level, never call it Level 4 or exceptional, and never describe it as measured or guaranteed output. Use the figure once, in the bass paragraph, where it adds substance; name Parameter 14 in full at most once and keep the prose natural. Match each benefit to its frozen evidence and supported channel family. Where only bass output is a selected strength, describe the weight and impact of low-frequency effects. Keep P14 bass output, P18 extension, P19 response at the reference position and P20 consistency across seats distinct; describe each only from its own supported evidence. No absolute guarantees and no unnecessary qualifications.
sections.requirement: Explain supported headroom for demanding film soundtracks, controlled reproduction of dynamic peaks and clear, confident presentation at the designed listening levels, using only the frozen dynamic-range evidence for each option and channel family. Keep bass output, extension, response at the reference position and consistency across seats distinct, each supported by its own evidence. No absolute guarantees.

sections.title: Timbre Matching
sections.requirement_single: Explain the tonal benefit the client will hear: voices, music and effects keeping a familiar tonal character as the soundtrack develops, and a similarly balanced presentation across the seating area, with the primary listening positions the priority. State what that consistency gives them where they sit, and why it matters as a soundtrack moves around the cinema. State the tonal aim as the design's own approach, and state the measured tonal consistency only for the speaker group the evidence states it for, across only the seats that result covers. These frequency-response results state how consistently ONE loudspeaker group holds its own tonal balance from seat to seat, so they are never evidence that one group of loudspeakers matches another: never write a screen-to-surround or any other between-group match, and never attach their figures to a comparison between the screen, the surround and the overhead speakers. Natural handover wording is welcome as the design's own aim: describe a voice or an effect keeping its character as the loudspeakers hand it on, and let that stand as intent rather than as a measured match between the groups. Keep every seat statement explicitly limited to tonal character, not overall balance, bass or placement. Never imply the design's loudspeaker package differs from another option's, and never broaden tonal consistency into equal seats or an equal whole experience. No bass-extension detour and no both parameters wording.
sections.requirement: Explain the loudspeaker and coverage evidence the pack records, and claim nothing beyond it. Where the copy describes a sound passing between loudspeakers, that is tonal continuity within the design and the design's own aim, never a claim that the loudspeaker package differs between the options and never a match measured between the speaker groups. The tonal results the pack carries are seat-to-seat frequency-response results, one speaker group each, so they are never used to claim that one group of loudspeakers matches another.

sections.title: Presented Options
sections.requirement_single: Where the brief supplies seating or layout options, present them in 2–3 natural sentences as practical alternatives within ONE design: what each arrangement gives the room, what it is like to sit in, how it looks and how it arranges the space. Describe the practical and visual differences the client is choosing between, in terms of comfort, seating style, appearance and the practical arrangement of the room, and where the pack states the seating dimensions, the sightlines or the clearance around the loudspeakers, use them to describe the arrangement rather than inventing one. State that each arrangement works within the seating positions this design specifies, and that the final choice rests on comfort and personal preference. Never state or imply that the options give identical, unchanged or equivalent acoustic performance, never introduce an acoustic-performance qualification of your own, and never present an option as a performance difference or a performance gain: where the copy states something about an area of the evidence it cites the allowed claim that supports it, and where the evidence supports nothing it is not written. Where the brief supplies no option, return an empty string for this section.
sections.requirement: Where the pack supplies option guidance, present the options it describes in 2–3 natural sentences as practical alternatives within one design, describing each arrangement in terms of comfort, seating style, appearance and the practical arrangement of the room, and state plainly what the choice rests on. Never state or imply that the options give identical, unchanged or equivalent acoustic performance, and never introduce an acoustic-performance qualification of your own. Where the pack supplies no option guidance, return an empty string for this section.

sections.title: Overall Design
sections.requirement_single: Close on what the client should expect from the final design: connect this particular picture and viewing experience to the movement around and above the audience, the tonal character, and the supported bass and dynamic strengths, in this project's own terms rather than a general claim. Do not repeat any number, specification list or earlier sentence. Never claim a consistent overall experience for every viewer from tonal evidence. Close by bringing the design together: why these choices suit this particular cinema and what they give the client, written as the designer's own considered judgement rather than a summary of what the other sections have already said, and never as an announcement that the design is recommended.

The low-frequency system adds another layer of authority, reaching deep enough to give the biggest effects genuine physical weight.

This system has exceptional low-frequency capability, combining very high output with infrasonic depth. The biggest effects have genuine physical scale and authority, creating the contrast between quiet detail and explosive moments that makes a cinema soundtrack exciting.

opening.rule: DYNAMIC RANGE OPENS ON THE CLIENT EXPERIENCE, NEVER ON A RESULT. The pillar opens with ONE whole-system statement of what the system does as the soundtrack moves from quiet detail to a major peak — the consequence the client hears — and only then is that statement supported by the system's own evidence: the screen-channel capability, the surround capability, the low-frequency output, the bass depth and the bass control, woven into the story as they naturally arise rather than listed one after another. design_rationale.rule: THE SEATING DECISION IS EXPLAINED AS A DESIGN REASON, NEVER AS A RESULT. Where the evidence carries a seating rationale, explain WHY the seating sits where it does: the space behind the seating is deliberate, the seats are kept clear of the rear wall because a seat close to it is one of the most difficult places in a room for bass and it affects how evenly the system behaves at the listening positions, and the clearance also leaves a better relationship between the audience and the surrounding loudspeakers. client_story_pillars.question: Can the system go from quiet dialogue and detail to large-scale impact without sounding strained?
client_story_pillars.why_care: Dynamic Range creates excitement. The low-frequency system adds another layer of authority, reaching deep enough to give the biggest effects genuine physical weight.

This system has exceptional low-frequency capability, combining very high output with infrasonic depth. The biggest effects have genuine physical scale and authority, creating the contrast between quiet detail and explosive moments that makes a cinema soundtrack exciting.

seating_clearance.the_two_measurements: the distance to the nearest room boundary and the distance to the wall behind the seating are two different measurements: the nearest boundary may be a side wall, the front wall or the rear wall, and neither distance is ever inferred from the other
seating_clearance.principle: Seating set close to a room boundary carries four practical compromises. The room's own low-frequency behaviour interacts with the nearby wall, so the bass can differ more from one seat to the next. Reflections returning from that wall arrive sooner and stronger, which softens clarity and the sense of space. The listener sits closer to the surrounding loudspeakers, so the system wraps around the audience less evenly. And the difference between one seat and the next grows. Providing suitable clearance helps reduce all four, so the seating position is part of the acoustic design rather than a matter of fitting seats into the room.
compromises: uneven bass response, because the room's own low-frequency behaviour interacts with the wall the listener sits near
stronger early reflections from the nearby wall, which affect clarity and spatial presentation
less separation between the listener and the surrounding loudspeakers, because the seat has less room around it
greater differences in the listening experience between seating positions
seating_clearance.limits: Clearance is a design measure rather than a result: it reduces those compromises and never guarantees a particular bass response, a particular measured outcome or a better design overall. A room can be seated clear of every wall and still be limited elsewhere, and a closer seat can be the right answer where the viewing geometry or the client's priorities call for it.

comparison_reading.rule: the comparison reading is the Stage 1 interpretation of what the options share and what changes between them. Alongside the designer's brief, it is the primary authority for the NARRATIVE PURPOSE of the comparison: what each design is for and how the room would be used. Engineering evidence remains the authority for every technical and performance claim. Do not recommend one option over another because it has higher RP22 scores, a larger speaker system, a larger screen or a higher price: a genuine engineering difference is stated objectively and never makes one option universally preferable. Recommend one option only where the designer's stated brief gives a clear priority that supports that recommendation; where it does not, present the options as credible alternatives without choosing a winner. The designer's text is context and guidance, never wording to copy, and no client preference, room use, design feature or performance claim is ever invented.

narrative_steer.rule: NARRATIVE PREFERENCES ARE INGREDIENTS, NOT A SECTION PLAN: the preferred topics below are subjects the designer wants weighed more heavily IF they help tell this project's story naturally. They are never requirements. Never write one paragraph per preferred topic, never work through them in order, never give one a heading, and never force a figure, a parameter or a claim into the copy because its subject was preferred. A preferred topic may appear briefly, in passing, combined with another point, or not at all where forcing it would damage the writing. The document is ONE coherent story about this cinema: where a preference fits it, give it more weight than a less relevant part of the evidence; where it does not fit, write the better account without it. A preference never adds a claim, widens a scope, promotes a weak or unremarkable result, or turns a result the client asked for into a headline. Where the designer's own brief addresses a subject, the brief is the stronger authority and these preferences change nothing about that answer. Where a preferred topic names a DECISION the designer made about this room rather than an achieved result — the room's orientation, the screen scale that decision released, the spacing left around the seating — explain WHY that decision was made, from the design reasons you are given, and never present it as a result: it carries no figure, no level and no measured outcome, and it is never a performance headline.
narrative_steer.exclude_rule: EXCLUDED TOPICS ARE KEPT OUT OF THE NARRATIVE: a topic the designer marked "do not discuss" is not written about in any client-facing section. Do not explain it, do not illustrate it with a figure, and do not build a story around it. This is a statement about copy alone: it changes no evidence, no reported result, no table and no figure of the document, and where the design has no other way to describe the room, describe what the client hears and move on.
narrative_steer.neutral_note: topics with no state recorded are neither preferred nor excluded: decide from the design story whether they are worth raising
