source.document: CEDIA/CTA-RP22 Immersive Audio Design Recommended Practice

rp22_design_context.rule: this is professional design context for explaining why a design decision suits this room. It is never engineering evidence, it states no figure, level, product or performance result, and it never establishes what this project has achieved: an established principle explains why an approach is normally used, a recorded designer explanation is why this design uses it, and the result this design achieved is read only from the frozen evidence. Every figure, level, product and claim still comes from the frozen evidence pack, and the frozen evidence governs wherever the two differ

principles.title: Holistic design and intelligent compromises
principles.principle: A cinema is designed as one system: the decisions interact and improving one objective can constrain another, so the design is revisited as a whole. The best performing systems are the ones with the most intelligent set of compromises, and the aim is performance balanced against practicality, aesthetics and cost.
principles.limitations: It establishes that a trade-off may be intelligent. It never establishes that a particular lower result WAS a deliberate compromise, and never that a compromise is acceptable to the client.
principles.project_evidence: The interpretation record: the constraints, the priorities, the strongest results, and the lower results it states a reason for.
principles.safe_use: Explain the balance the design strikes and why the combination suits this room. Name a trade-off as deliberate only where the interpretation or the designer records a reason for it; otherwise state the result and stop.

principles.title: Surround quantity and multi-row positioning
principles.principle: The surround and rear speakers are placed to carry sound around the audience, and the placement has to work for the whole seating area rather than one seat. Their positions within the recommended zones are what creates continuous movement; more speakers at poorer positions do not.
principles.applicability: Applies where the design has a bed layout of five channels or more.
principles.limitations: A channel count never establishes smooth movement, and a position assessed as limited is not explained by the count.
principles.project_evidence: The frozen layout and bed channel count, the recorded speaker positions, and the assessed horizontal spacing and placement results.
principles.safe_use: Explain how the arrangement carries sound around and past the audience. Where a spacing result is limited, describe it as the practical speaker positions and the seating geometry setting the result, and claim no more than the assessed result supports.

principles.title: Front-wide loudspeaker purpose
principles.principle: Front wides bridge the angular gap between the screen channels and the side surrounds, so that sound travelling across the front of the room passes through the room rather than jumping from the screen to the side walls. Whether the ideal position is available depends on the room: a doorway, an opening or the furniture can constrain it.
principles.applicability: Applies where the design has front-wide speakers.
principles.limitations: It never establishes why a wide ended up where it is, and a constrained position is a geometry outcome rather than a fault in the design.
principles.project_evidence: The recorded front-wide positions, the assessed front-wide placement result, and any recorded room element or designer note that constrains the wall.
principles.safe_use: Explain what the wides contribute to movement between the screen and the sides. Where the evidence records a compromise and the designer records the reason, state it plainly; where no reason is recorded, state the outcome and write no reason.

principles.title: Overhead quantity, positioning and the listening area
principles.principle: The upper speakers are positioned to serve the shape and extent of the listening area, and the number of them is adapted to that area rather than chosen for a format label. The arrangement, not the label, is what places sound above the audience.
principles.applicability: Applies where the design has one or more overhead channels.
principles.limitations: A layout label is never evidence that every seat receives the same overhead coverage, and an overhead count is never evidence of why that count was chosen.
principles.project_evidence: The frozen overhead channel count and layout, the recorded overhead positions, the seating geometry and the assessed overhead spacing result.
principles.safe_use: Explain that the overhead arrangement is set out to cover the seating area, using the assessed spacing result where it exists. Never state a coverage outcome from the count alone, and never explain the count as a deliberate choice unless the designer records one.

principles.title: Speaker selection, dispersion and timbre
principles.principle: Speaker performance is judged by how the loudspeaker behaves off axis as well as on it, because the audience hears the off-axis response as much as the direct sound. Similar spectral and phase behaviour across the channels is what lets a voice or an effect keep its character as it moves from one loudspeaker to another.
principles.applicability: Applies where the design has assessed timbre or spectral results, or recorded loudspeaker selections.
principles.limitations: Sharing a manufacturer or a series is not evidence of a measured timbre match, and a nominal dispersion figure is not a room-level coverage verification.
principles.project_evidence: The assessed timbre and spectral results, and the recorded loudspeaker selections the reports state.
principles.safe_use: Explain why consistent tonal character matters as sound moves around the cinema, using the assessed timbre result. Describe tonal continuity as a loudspeaker handing a voice or an effect on, and never widen it into equal seats or an equal whole experience.

principles.title: Subwoofer quantity, positioning and room modes
principles.principle: The objective with low frequencies is for the level and response to be consistent across all seats with no audible resonances, which is a different aim from a flat response at one seat or a couple more decibels of output. Room modes make the response differ from seat to seat, so the subwoofer arrangement and the seating positions are chosen together, and additional subwoofers arranged and aligned deliberately can reduce that variation.
principles.applicability: Applies where the design has one or more subwoofers.
principles.limitations: A subwoofer count never establishes seat-to-seat consistency, and a multi-subwoofer arrangement is a method rather than a proven outcome: the reasoning behind the approach is explained positively, while the result this design achieved is stated only where the bass evidence states it.
principles.project_evidence: The frozen subwoofer count and the recorded arrangement, the assessed bass results the reports publish, the scope each of those results is stated at, and any designer explanation the project records for the arrangement.
principles.safe_use: Explain the bass approach and what the published bass result states at its own scope, and explain the reasoning behind the arrangement itself positively and confidently: spreading low-frequency sources around the room is a recognised way to reduce the influence of the room modes that make one seat differ from another, and that reasoning holds whatever the project's own consistency result turns out to be. Where the designer has recorded why the arrangement was chosen, develop that reasoning properly rather than paraphrasing it. Explain a principle or an intention as the reasoning behind the design, and never as a result this design has achieved: claim seat-to-seat consistency only where the consistency result itself supports it, and never present the arrangement as having produced a consistency the evidence does not state. The reasoning behind the arrangement rests on established acoustic practice and the designer's recorded intention, while a statement of the output the subwoofers provide is supported by the authoritative performance evidence: both belong in one natural explanation of the bass approach, combined as the subject reads best, and never split into separate sentences, separate paragraphs or prescribed transitions.

principles.title: Physical design before electronic optimisation
principles.principle: Room dimensions, the seating positions and the subwoofer positions are the physical design; equalisation is applied afterwards and cannot make every physical arrangement equivalent. Room correction works with a suitable physical design rather than replacing it.
principles.applicability: Applies where the design has one or more subwoofers.
principles.limitations: It is never evidence that a design has been calibrated, that a room has been measured, or that a predicted result has been achieved in the room.
principles.project_evidence: The frozen room and seating geometry, the recorded subwoofer positions, and whether the engineering authority states an applied calibration.
principles.safe_use: Explain that the physical arrangement has been designed for this room and this geometry, and state what it provides for the design. Never describe a design-stage prediction as a measured or commissioned result, and never append a verification disclaimer to the capability it provides.

acoustics_policy.statement: Sound Proof is principally a design-stage tool: the room may not yet exist, so acoustic absorption, reflection decay, background noise and sound isolation may be estimated or assumed rather than measured.
rules: acoustic absorption, reflection decay, background noise and sound isolation are not prominent subjects in a normal client proposal: mention one only where the frozen evidence makes it relevant to a decision the design already records
never imply that specified acoustic treatment has already achieved a particular acoustic result
never describe an assumed P15 or P21 level as measured, as achieved, or as a result of anything: it is an assumption recorded by the designer
a specified treatment quantity is a design decision, never evidence of the acoustic outcome it was specified for
where the room has not been measured, the copy states the design as designed and claims no measured acoustic outcome

treatment_guidance.applies_when: the frozen bass assessment identifies a problem that suitable acoustic treatment might help address
rules: suggest a potential benefit only where it is consistent with the frequencies involved and the known treatment data, and keep the suggestion restrained
never guarantee an improvement, and never promise that treatment will resolve the problem
never claim an improved P19 or P20 result from acoustic treatment unless the engineering model actually evaluates and supports that improvement
never embellish acoustic-treatment benefits, and never describe treatment as delivering a result the assessment does not state
treatment is offered as something to consider within the design, never as an instruction to change the finished design and never as a next step the client must take

evidence_safety: RP22 explains general design principles. It explains why an approach is normally used, and it never establishes why a particular designer selected a configuration: a recorded designer explanation is why this design uses it.
never infer a design decision from an equipment count: a channel count, an overhead count or a subwoofer count is evidence of what the design contains, never of why it was chosen
keep RP22 guidance, verified project engineering, designer-supplied intentions and approved master-admin knowledge separate: none of them stands in for another

keep the three forms of knowledge apart. An established principle explains why an approach is used and is written confidently. A designer's recorded intention is the reasoning behind this design and is written confidently: it does not become invalid because a parameter scored low, and it is never weakened, hedged or apologised for because of one. A calculated result states what this design achieved, and it is never exaggerated, widened or replaced by a principle. Neither a principle nor an intention is ever turned into a project-specific guarantee, and none of them is repeated as a defensive qualification after every statement
an applicable principle is context for explaining the design; it is never a result, a level, a score, a measurement or a performance claim
where the frozen evidence records no reason for a decision, state the design and its result, and write no reason at all

the context strengthens the explanation of the recommended system and never introduces a verification disclaimer: a capability is stated confidently from the frozen evidence, and calibration or commissioning is mentioned only where the client's brief raises it or where it is an important practical recommendation

clarification_answers.rule: Clarification answers are the designer's own statements of design intention for a decision the frozen evidence records no reason for. Weave each answer into the section it belongs to (its belongs_to), in your own words and in the document's professional voice. Never print the question, never label the answer, never present the answer as a standalone statement or as a list, and never treat it as measured engineering evidence: it is intention only, it changes no figure, level, product or claim, and the frozen evidence governs wherever the two differ. Understand the technical meaning of each answer and develop it properly with established acoustic knowledge, so the reasoning behind the decision is explained confidently and usefully rather than paraphrased: an intention is never weakened, hedged or apologised for because a parameter scored low, and it is never given a figure, a level or a guarantee of its own. The answer is the REASON and never the copy: never quote it, never repeat its wording, and never carry its shorthand, abbreviation or engineering jargon into the document. Restate the reasoning in the document's own professional language, as the designer would explain the decision to the client, so a phrase that is useful between engineers is never printed at the client: a term that names a mechanism rather than an experience — a gap left in a layer, a hole in the coverage — is replaced by what the listener hears and what the decision does about it. Where an answer explains a choice through a practical constraint on the room — how the room is used, the space a furnishing, a thoroughfare or a storage area occupies, what happens at one end of the room — explain the design's RESPONSE to that constraint, in general terms. The constraint is the context for the decision, never a requirement: never state a furnishing, a joinery item, a bar or any other interior feature as something the design needs, specifies or depends on. Where the designer passed a question there is no answer at all, and no reason may be invented for it.

evidence_classification.rule: keep these classes apart: a design fact is stated as what the design is, a supported result is the only source of a performance benefit, a designer intention is never an achievement, a prediction is never written as done, and an unknown or unsupported outcome is never written at all

classes.confirmed_design_fact: the design as it is built (evidence_pack.options[].facts: room, display, seating, system): state it as what the design is
classes.supported_engineering_result: a graded result the frozen reports state, carried as an allowed claim: the only source of a performance benefit
classes.established_design_principle: how acoustics and system design work, and why an approach is normally used (the RP22 design context): explained confidently as the reasoning behind the design, never as a result this design has achieved, and never given a figure, a level or a project-specific guarantee
classes.designer_intention: what the designer set out to do (editorial_brief, design_interpretation.design_decisions, clarification_answers): an intention, never an achieved outcome, and written as confident rationale: a lower result elsewhere never invalidates it and never forces a hedge
classes.prediction: what the design is expected to do before it is built: never written as a result the design has delivered
classes.unknown_or_unsupported: what no source states (blocked_claims, design_interpretation.unknown_or_unsupported): never written, in any wording

principles.rule: an established design principle and a recorded designer intention are explained confidently as the reasoning behind an approach; a supported result is the only statement of what this design achieved, and it is never widened, replaced or guaranteed by a principle

bass.rule: P19 is stated at the reference seating position only; a claimed seat-to-seat bass consistency needs the pack's own whole-seat positively-graded P20 result, and weak or absent P20 evidence never supports one

options.note: the frozen reports publish the bass result: each bass benefit cites its own allowed claim
the frozen reports publish the bass result: each bass benefit cites its own allowed claim

multi_cabinet_channels.rule: Explain each required frozen arrangement naturally once in the System Design Summary or specification: the physical cabinet count, the position and the ONE logical audio channel. In comparisons name the appropriate design; never assign its arrangement to another option. This is a concise design explanation, not an equipment inventory.

timbre_metric_authority.rule: P16 and P17 are seat-to-seat frequency-response results: each states how consistently ONE loudspeaker group holds its own tonal balance from listening position to listening position. Neither states how closely one loudspeaker group resembles another, so a seat-to-seat figure is never written as an inter-speaker or between-group match, and is never attached to a comparison between the screen, surround and overhead speakers. The tonal aim of the design is written as the aim it is: where the copy describes a sound keeping its character as it passes between loudspeakers, that is the design's intent, never a measured match between the speaker groups and never a figure from these results.

metrics.metric: seat-to-seat frequency-response variance across the screen-wall speakers, normalised to the measured response at the reference seating position (500 Hz to 16 kHz, one-octave smoothing)
metrics.establishes: how consistently the screen channels hold the same tonal balance from seat to seat
metrics.does_not_establish: a match between the screen channels and any other loudspeaker group

metrics.metric: seat-to-seat frequency-response variance across the wide, surround and upper speakers, normalised to the measured response at the reference seating position (500 Hz to 16 kHz, one-octave smoothing)
metrics.establishes: how consistently the surround and overhead speakers hold the same tonal balance from seat to seat
metrics.does_not_establish: a match between the surround or overhead speakers and any other loudspeaker group

client_story_pillars.core_rule: ASDR tells us what matters. RP22 tells us how well it performs. The brief tells us whether that performance is right for this project. The three pillars tell us how to explain why the client should care.
client_story_pillars.hierarchy_rule: THE STORY RUNS: brief, then ASDR importance, then the evidence, then the three pillars, then the client's experience. It never runs parameter, paragraph, next parameter.
client_story_pillars.method_rule: FOR EVERY IMPORTANT RESULT OR GROUP OF RELATED RESULTS, ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS BEFORE WRITING: (1) which of the three pillars does this strengthen? (2) what does that change in the listening experience? (3) why should the client care? Write from answers 2 and 3. The parameter numbers remain evidence.
client_story_pillars.structure_rule: THE THREE PILLARS ORGANISE THE CLIENT STORY: Dynamic Range, Spatial Resolution and Timbre Matching. They are the performance characteristics Sound Proof says make a system good, and they are the structure the client story is written through. RP22 parameters are the evidence underneath them, never the structure: do not make individual parameters the shape of the client story, do not give a parameter its own section, heading or paragraph, and never produce "Bass Output / Bass Extension / Bass Response / Bass Consistency" as four stories. Produce Dynamic Range as one fluent story about the WHOLE system — the front stage and dialogue staying clear, the surrounds keeping up as the mix becomes demanding, and the bass giving those moments their scale and weight — with the control and consistency of that experience supporting it where the evidence holds.
client_story_pillars.evidence_rule: NEVER MERELY REPORT THE EVIDENCE. Do not write "99 dBC", "26 Hz" or "Level 3" as the point of a sentence. Explain what those results collectively allow the system to do: the contrast it preserves, the scale it gives the biggest moments, the space it places effects in, the character it keeps as sound moves. A figure earns its place only where it states a key result the client asked about.
client_story_pillars.bass_rule: THE BASS IS ONE LAYER OF THE DYNAMIC RANGE STORY, NEVER THE SUBJECT OF ITS OWN. Bass output, bass depth, the response at the reference position and the consistency across the seating are readings of one thing the client experiences as a single subject, so they are combined into the Dynamic Range story rather than discussed independently — and they are never the whole of that story. A strong bass system is not "26 Hz" or "P14 L3": it is a greater contrast between quiet material and the largest effects, with the deepest moments having scale and physical weight. P19 supports the control and quality of that experience at the reference position and P20 how well it carries across the seating: name neither as a parameter, and tell both inside the same bass account.
client_story_pillars.dynamic_range_rule: DYNAMIC RANGE IS A WHOLE-SYSTEM STORY, NEVER A BASS STORY. It describes the contrast between quiet detail and the largest moments the COMPLETE system can reproduce cleanly. Before writing it, read the whole system and answer these for THIS project: can dialogue and quiet detail remain clear? can the front stage produce major peaks cleanly? can the surrounds keep up when the soundtrack becomes busy? does the bass system provide the scale and physical weight underneath those peaks? and how impressive is that contrast for this project's brief? Then write ONE Dynamic Range story from those answers, covering the front stage, the surrounds and the bass together: a Dynamic Range story that describes only the subwoofers is wrong, however strong that bass is. Inside the pillar, high-weight results carry the emphasis and low-weight results never dominate it, and the bass may lead where it is genuinely the strongest and most relevant part of the design — the pillar still describes the performance of the SYSTEM. Where the system is modest for its brief, write it honestly and positively for the room it is in: never pretend reference cinema output, and never apologise for it either.
client_story_pillars.opening_rule: DYNAMIC RANGE OPENS ON THE CLIENT EXPERIENCE, NEVER ON A RESULT. The pillar opens with ONE whole-system statement of what the system does as the soundtrack moves from quiet detail to a major peak — the consequence the client hears — and only then is that statement supported by the system's own evidence: the screen-channel capability, the surround capability, the low-frequency output, the bass depth and the bass control, woven into the story as they naturally arise rather than listed one after another. The opening is read from Dynamic Range's own opening claim, at the strength the system's carrying results have earned. THE RESULT LEVELS DECIDE HOW STRONG THAT CLAIM MAY BE AND WHICH LAYER IS EMPHASISED; THEY NEVER DECIDE THE SENTENCE ORDER. The whole-system claim is a claim about the system's dynamic headroom, so it is read at the WEAKEST of the layers that carry that headroom — the screen channels, the surrounds and the low-frequency output: a whole-system claim is only as strong as the least capable part of the system that carries it, and no single strong layer escalates it. The bass depth and the bass control are TOLD AND EMPHASISED AT THE LEVEL THEIR OWN RESULTS EARNED, and they never hold the headroom claim down. The highest-level result never automatically becomes the opening sentence, the bass never opens the pillar by default, and the front stage never opens it by default: where one layer carries the strongest result, it is given the greatest EMPHASIS inside the story rather than the first sentence by right. Where the system is modest for its brief, the opening says so positively, in the language that brief supports. THE TIER DECIDES HOW STRONG THE CLAIM IS; THE PROJECT'S OWN INTENT DECIDES THE LANGUAGE IT IS TOLD IN: the same achieved strength is opened in the vocabulary the room supports — a media room in relaxed everyday-viewing terms, a dedicated cinema in cinema terms — and the vocabulary never raises or lowers the strength, so brief-sensitive wording is never used to inflate or soften a result.
client_story_pillars.opening_weave_rule: THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS THE OPENING, IT DOES NOT REPLACE IT. The screen-channel capability, the surround capability, the low-frequency output, the bass depth and the bass control are woven into the opening statement as they naturally arise — the front stage and the surrounds as the soundtrack becomes demanding, the bass underneath those moments — and never listed one after another as separate talking points. The opening sentence states what the client hears; the evidence behind it is what makes that statement true.
client_story_pillars.opening_field: pillars[].opening — the opening claim, the strength it was read from, the layer to emphasise and the evidence to support it with
client_story_pillars.cross_pillar_rule: ONE RESULT MAY STRENGTHEN MORE THAN ONE CLIENT EXPERIENCE. Bass output and physical scale reinforce Dynamic Range, while the quality of the bass response and its seat-to-seat consistency reinforce the consistency the client hears in the low-frequency character, so the bass is told where the experience it changes belongs and is never forced into a single narrative box. Technical RP22 categorisation is unchanged by this: a parameter's engineering classification stays exactly what the evidence states, and only the CLIENT story is written across the pillars.
client_story_pillars.brief_rule: THE BRIEF DECIDES WHETHER A RESULT IS A SUCCESS. Never judge success from an RP22 Performance Level alone: a single-row 5.1 television lounge may achieve L1 or L2 in high-weight parameters and still be a highly successful design, because that performance is right for the intended use. The same results in a reference-quality twelve-seat dedicated cinema may be a limitation. Read the brief and the intended use first, describe a result that suits the project positively as the achievement it is, and never present a result as strong, weak, generous or limited without that context.
client_story_pillars.seat_scope_rule: PRESERVE THE EXACT SEAT SCOPE. Where the bass consistency result holds for the primary seats only, say "across the primary seating area" and stop there: never claim all-seat consistency, never write "across the room", "across every seat" or "throughout the room", and never let the shared-experience sentence imply a seat it does not hold for. Where the result holds across the assessed seating, the wider wording is allowed. The seats a claim is made for are read from the result itself, never chosen for emphasis.
client_story_pillars.infrasonic_rule: INFRASONIC LANGUAGE MUST BE EARNED. Use "infrasonic", or phrases such as infrasonic depth, physical scale, felt as much as heard or genuine low-frequency authority, ONLY where the bass extension result genuinely supports it: a moderate or mid-band extension is written as the depth it gives the soundtrack, with no infrasonic claim and no promise below the published limit. Do not hedge a deep result either.
client_story_pillars.infrasonic_example: The system reaches into the infrasonic part of the soundtrack, adding a physical sense of scale to the biggest effects as well as audible bass.
client_story_pillars.seating_note: THE SEATING IS A DESIGN DECISION, NOT A FOURTH PILLAR. Where the seating arrangement is explained, explain in plain terms what the placement does for the listener: the room working with the seating, the viewing position, and the balance the layout strikes. It is never presented as a performance result, never given a Performance Level, and never turned into a pillar of its own.
client_story_pillars.seating_rationale_rule: THE SEATING DECISION IS EXPLAINED AS A DESIGN REASON, NEVER AS A RESULT. Where the evidence carries a seating rationale, explain WHY the seating sits where it does: the space behind the seating is deliberate, the seats are kept clear of the rear wall because a seat close to it is one of the most difficult places in a room for bass and it affects how evenly the system behaves at the listening positions, and the clearance also leaves a better relationship between the audience and the surrounding loudspeakers. It is a deliberate design decision rather than wasted floor space. State no parameter, no Performance Level and no equation, never quote the distance as if it were the benefit, and never promise a particular measured bass outcome. Where the room takes a compromise, explain the balance constructively. Where the seating subject is steered do-not-discuss, the rationale is not written at all.
client_story_pillars.always_available_rule: A PILLAR IS NEVER SILENCED BY ITS OWN EVIDENCE. Dynamic Range, Spatial Resolution and Timbre Matching are the three ways Sound Proof explains performance, and every proposal tells all three. ASDR importance decides how much of the EVIDENCE beneath a pillar is discussed — which results lead, which support and which stay in the engineering evidence — and never whether the pillar itself is there. Where little beneath a pillar is worth telling, that pillar is simply shorter: write it briefly and honestly from the evidence it does hold, without leaving it out, apologising for it or padding it.
client_story_pillars.emphasis_rule: THE EMPHASIS INSIDE A PILLAR IS ALREADY DECIDED. Each result beneath a pillar carries an emphasis: a lead result is written out; a supporting or contributing result is woven into the same story; a context result strengthens the pillar but belongs in the engineering evidence, so it is mentioned only in passing where the story genuinely needs it. A lightly weighted result that happens to score highly is never a headline, and a heavily weighted result is discussed even where its level is modest. Never re-rank the evidence and never invent an emphasis.
client_story_pillars.lead_rule: TWO LEVELS OF IMPORTANCE, NEVER ONE. The GLOBAL narrative priority decides how much space a subject gets in the proposal overall: it comes from ASDR weight, brief relevance and the designer's steer, and it is what makes one pillar the dominant story. The PILLAR EVIDENCE PRIORITY decides which result leads each pillar: inside every pillar, the strongest result that may be told at all is that pillar's lead evidence, and it is written in the strong language its own achieved result has earned, whatever its global rank. A pillar is never demoted because another pillar's evidence is heavier, and a pillar's lead evidence never becomes the whole proposal's dominant story on its own: excellent evidence inside a quieter pillar is told well and briefly, in proportion to that pillar's overall place in the story. Scale the language from the achieved result; scale the space from the global narrative priority.
client_story_pillars.seat_narration_rule: WHERE THE SEATING IS NOT NARRATED, THE RESULT STILL IS. Where the designer has ruled the seating out of the narrative, a pillar's lead evidence is still stated for what it is: give it to the loudspeaker group or the layer it belongs to — the tonal consistency of the screen channels, the tonal consistency of the surround and height layers, the placement and movement of sound in the room. Do not name seats, rows, the primary or secondary seats, the reference listening position or the seating geometry, and never invent a non-seating claim the evidence does not support. The two tonal results are consistency within their own loudspeaker group, one group each: they are never written as a comparison measured between the two groups.
client_story_pillars.seat_narration_applies_when: a pillar carries seat_narration: "banned" — the designer has ruled the seating out of the narrative

pillars.label: Dynamic Range
pillars.question: Can the system go from quiet dialogue and detail to large-scale impact without sounding strained?
pillars.why_care: Dynamic Range creates excitement. A system with good dynamic range stays clear and relaxed through quiet material and then produces genuine scale and impact when the soundtrack demands it: the contrast between quiet detail and explosive moments is where the excitement, the realism and the musical energy come from.

pillars.label: Spatial Resolution
pillars.question: Can sounds appear in convincing places and move naturally around the room?
pillars.why_care: Because dialogue stays connected to the picture and effects create a believable space instead of sounding like individual speakers. The loudspeakers disappear more easily as sources, and the soundtrack forms a space around the audience that the client can follow.
translation: the connection between sound and picture
the ability to follow an effect around the room

pillars.label: Timbre Matching
pillars.question: Does a voice, an instrument or an effect retain its character as it moves between speakers and seats?
pillars.why_care: Because the system sounds like one coherent environment rather than a collection of different loudspeakers. Attention stays on the film or the music instead of on differences between the loudspeakers or between the seats.
translation: effects not changing tone as they move
a broadly similar tonal balance across the important seating positions

bass_parts.question: How much output is available for the largest moments?
bass_parts.notices: the largest effects have something substantial to draw on

bass_parts.question: How low does the system reach, and how much scale does that give the deepest moments?
bass_parts.notices: the deepest moments have scale and physical weight rather than simply getting louder

bass_parts.question: How closely does the response follow the target at the reference seating position?
bass_parts.notices: the weight arrives cleanly instead of smearing the detail above it

bass_parts.question: How well does that bass performance carry across the primary seats?
bass_parts.notices: the weight and excitement are shared rather than concentrated in one seat

system_parts.question: Can dialogue and quiet detail remain clear, and can the front stage produce the major peaks cleanly?
system_parts.notices: dialogue and fine detail stay clear while the front stage takes the biggest peaks in its stride

system_parts.question: Can the surrounds keep up when the soundtrack becomes busy?
system_parts.notices: the whole soundtrack keeps its energy as the mix becomes demanding

client_story_pillars.source: the canonical pillar grouping, over the same classified evidence as strength_stories

writing_rules: Write only from the evidence pack. It is the sole source of every fact, figure, level and claim.

The ranked strength stories you are given decide which engineering characteristics deserve emphasis: rank 1 is the strongest result the evidence states, and never decide for yourself which parameters matter. The ranking is not a compulsory order for the document: the design's own story sets the editorial order, and every story you state is stated by citing its own allowed_claim_ids.

A verified ADI design interpretation is supplied in design_interpretation: the room, its intended use, the display and seating, the system architecture, the constraints, the reasons behind the design decisions, the strongest characteristics and the results that are reliable evidence. Read it and write from it. It explains the design and is never a source of figures: every figure, level, parameter and product still comes from the evidence pack and its allowed claims, the frozen evidence takes priority wherever the two differ, and where the interpretation states nothing you invent nothing.

The designer's own brief is supplied in editorial_brief. Treat it as instructions about what to emphasise and what needs explaining. It never overrides the evidence, it never changes a figure, a level, a product or a claim, and it is never copied: no note, instruction, filename or caption from it appears in the draft.
Sell what the design delivers, not how it was analysed. This is the proposal stage: state the finished design and what the client will experience, never the design-stage work that produced it.

Open each story with the experience the client will have, then why they will value it, then the engineering proof. The number is the proof, never the story, so never lead a paragraph with a parameter number, a Performance Level, a channel count or a dB value.

Write the section the pack asks for under its own label: where the pack is a single-option proposal it carries no comparison headings, so write the design the client is being offered and why this specification was chosen, and never write filler such as "there are no changes to report".

Name the display exactly as the frozen evidence names it. Where the display is a TV, write the TV (for example 115" TV) and use it in the viewing story with the viewing angle and the front-row seating; never write a screen size, an aspect ratio, a viewable width or any projector word. A projection screen keeps its projector-screen language.

Never write in the software-report register: no "assessed for", "this parameter", "according to the report", "performance result", "this proposal details", "established configuration" or "calculated design result".

In a single-option proposal, never compare the design to a baseline or another option: no increase, greater, improved, more capable, additional headroom, higher output, upgrade or compared to. Describe the capability directly.

The proposal describes the design that has been specified and what it will deliver. Never write as though its performance has already been demonstrated in this room: the engineering analysis is complete and frozen, and the design is proposed, specified, modelled and designed.
This proposal is written before installation: write specified, selected, designed, modelled or proposed, never installed or installation, unless the frozen evidence says the system is installed.
Every client-facing claim must cite one or more allowed claim IDs in that section's claim_ids.

Where a section states what is shared and also contrasts the options, cite both: the shared-result claims for the unchanged facts and the factual-change or material-gain claims for the facts that differ.
Copy every figure, Performance Level and product name exactly as the pack states it. Never round, convert, restate or estimate.
Never name a product the pack does not list for the option it belongs to.

Read multi_cabinet_channels: where frozen evidence specifies multiple physical cabinets reproducing one logical audio channel, explain the exact cabinet count and the one channel naturally once in the System Design Summary or specification. Attribute the arrangement to its own design in a comparison. Accept natural wording, not an equipment inventory.

State supported dynamic-range benefits positively: headroom for demanding film soundtracks, controlled dynamic peaks and clear, confident presentation at the designed listening levels. Match each benefit to the frozen evidence and channel family; bass output is not bass extension, reference-position response or seat consistency.

Never publish internal claim-defence, validation, testing or scoring commentary. A practical qualification the client needs is still written: when presenting seating alternatives, state that each arrangement works within the seating positions this design specifies, and never turn that into a statement about acoustic performance.

Where the pack states a dual-centre screen stage, name the stage position by position: the left and right channels with their own model, and the centre with its own cabinet count and model (for example Front Left / Right: Q6-3 and Centre: 2 × C4-1 dual physical centre cabinets). Never write the three screen channels as one LCR of the left/right model, never write the centre as that model, and never write three loudspeakers of it: the centre is two physical cabinets fed from one centre channel, and the layout is unchanged.

Where the pack supplies option guidance, that guidance is the designer's instruction and never copy: write your own polished client-facing prose from it, and never reproduce a note, an instruction or a filename in the draft. Where the pack supplies no option guidance, return the presented_options section as an empty string and write nothing into it.

Present seating and layout options as practical alternatives within ONE design. Say what each arrangement gives the room in terms of comfort, seating style, appearance and the practical arrangement of the space, that each arrangement works within the seating positions this design specifies, and that the final choice rests on comfort and personal preference. Where the pack states the seating dimensions, the sightlines or the clearance around the loudspeakers, use them; never invent one. Never say or imply that the options give identical, unchanged or equivalent acoustic performance, never write an acoustic-performance qualification of your own, and never make a performance claim or a performance difference of a seating choice: where the copy states something about an area of the evidence it cites the allowed claim that supports it.
Never present a claim the pack blocks, and never describe a shared result as a change or a gain.
Never recommend changing the design, and never describe the proposal as an upgrade path.

Never reference an assumed or administrative check (P8 upfiring/elevation speakers, P15 background noise floor, P21 early reflections): where the pack records one as requested, state it once, label it as an assumption, and never use it as a result or a differentiator.
Where P20 does not support seat-to-seat bass consistency, describe bass only as output authority, physical capability and the subwoofer specification.
State a primary-seat or a secondary-seat result only where the pack states that scope's own claim, word it for that scope alone, and never present it as a result for the seating area or the room.
Sell what is strong: state a supported strength positively and stop there, and where one scope is the stronger, keep the claim to that scope rather than reporting the weaker one beside it.

The proposal is not a design review: never write that something needs attention, improvement, calibration, optimisation or further design work, and never suggest a future correction, a recalibration or an upgrade path.
Write to the client: benefit-led, dealer-safe language, with no internal parameter codes and no engineering jargon.

No sentence of 10 or more words may appear verbatim in more than one section. Do not reuse complete evidence sentences with minor word substitutions. Facts may recur only for a genuinely different editorial purpose.

Give each section its own job, and never carry the same three strengths through the document in the same words: Design Summary introduces the cinema; Design Overview explains how the system is arranged; Why This Specification explains why this solution suits the project; Key Performance Highlights sets out the engineering evidence; Spatial Resolution explains how the layout creates the immersion; Dynamic Range explains the capability and what it buys; Timbre Matching explains the tonal benefit; Overall Design closes on what the client should expect. Review the proposal as ONE document: every section contributes something the others do not, the closing Overall Design never restates the opening summary, and a repeated idea is acceptable only where it adds a genuinely different aspect of the design.

Use each engineering figure normally once in main prose. Keep output figures in Dynamic Range, viewing angles with the seating and display description (never in Spatial Resolution) and extension proof where it explains deep bass. Repeat only where it adds real value, never in Overall Design.
Never write L1, L2, L3, L4, L4 result or RP22 Level 4 in narrative prose. Never write (OH); write overhead channels. Structured grading tables and pills are not narrative prose.

Tonal consistency across seats supports only tonal character, and it is stated for the speaker group and the seats its own result covers: never broaden it into equal seats, overall experience balance, bass consistency, placement consistency or whole-room balance, and never write it as a match between the screen, surround and overhead loudspeakers.
Use the ranked story as evidence, not as a sentence to read aloud. Translate its meaning into natural client language while retaining its scope, exact facts and claim IDs.

Keep Appendix Notes brief, factual and source-only: this proposal is based on the frozen Project Report for this design, with detailed RP22, RP23, product and room evidence in the accompanying report. No sales story, acoustic-treatment performance promise or engineering-model explanation.

Close on this design's particular viewing experience, movement, tonal character and bass capability, not treats every seat as a priority, balances high-resolution spatial imaging with authoritative bass performance, high-quality experience for everyone or immersive and consistent experience for the home.

Tell the story, never the mechanism. Never use a channel count as a selling point ("5 discrete channels"), never name a feature or a layer the design does not include ("no overhead channels are specified"), and never explain how a mechanism works: no "reproduce the system's low-frequency content", and no account of what nearby walls, reflections or room modes do. Keep an exact boundary distance, a spacing, an angle and any other parameter number out of the Design Summary, the Design Overview, Key Performance Highlights and the closing narrative, where the client is reading a design explanation rather than a measurement. Say what the client hears, and let the evidence support that account rather than become it.
Keep every paragraph to one to three sentences, and keep every section inside its word limit.
Explain what each recorded result means for the room, rather than naming the number and moving on.

Where the brief asks for a result the pack carries as a supporting_result claim, state it in the section it belongs to, at exactly the scope, value and prediction status that claim carries, and cite its claim ID. A supporting result answers the client's own request: it is never presented as a strength, a headline or a comparison, and is never moved to a wider scope.

No contents sentence ("the following sections explain"), and no generic closing about the design as a whole: finish on what this particular cinema gives the client, and never repeat a benefit another section has already made.

Explain the professional judgement behind the design where the design_philosophy block records it: what the client wants to achieve, the prioritised listening positions, the display and seating balance, the constraints, the coverage and bass approaches, the strongest results, the lower results that are conscious trade-offs, and why the finished design suits the brief. Never invent a reason, a priority, a budget or a decision the interpretation does not record.

The best design is the one that most effectively satisfies the brief while balancing performance, practicality, aesthetics and cost, so a result below the highest available level is a legitimate design decision rather than a failure. Never present the highest available level as the objective regardless of cost or practical consequence, and never treat a higher price as better value on its own.

Value-engineering opportunities are internal reasoning, never copy: where the design already takes one, say what it gives the client; where one remains a design choice, say nothing about it. Never write an opportunity as an instruction to change the finished design, a next step, a future correction or an upgrade path.

Where the copy expresses the design team's own judgement or recommendation, write we or our. The engineering facts themselves stay stated as fact, we never stands in the place of a measured result, and no conversation, a meeting, a site visit or a client instruction the brief does not state is ever implied. Use it naturally and selectively, for example "We have prioritised", "Based on our understanding of the brief" or "In our experience with rooms like this", and never announce a recommendation: no "Our recommendation is" and no "We recommend".
Never infer that a design change improved a parameter unless the assessment supports it, never imply that every seat performs identically, and never state a benefit the evidence does not carry.

Never use an em dash (U+2014) anywhere in client-facing copy: punctuate the sentence another way or rewrite it naturally, and never alter a figure, a product identifier or an evidence reference while doing so. The draft carries zero em dashes.

Vary sentence structure and paragraph length, prefer direct active language, and use natural transitions. Never begin a sentence with Furthermore, Moreover, Additionally, Subsequently, In conclusion or It is important to note that, never open paragraph after paragraph on The system, The design, This ensures or The result, and never force a contraction into a formal passage.

Never use a generic marketing phrase ("sophisticated cinematic experience", "seamless immersive sound", "unparalleled performance", "delivers exceptional immersion", "elevates the listening experience", "brings everything together"): replace it with a project-specific explanation of what was chosen, why it suits this room, what the client gains and what the engineering supports, and never invent a reason to do it.

Before returning, read every section together as one document and refine the wording where it does not sound like a real cinema designer, where a sentence adds nothing, where a benefit is repeated, where a qualification is excessive or where the design intent is unclear. Never print that review, a note about a change or any explanation of your own editing.
Return structured JSON only, in every section this contract requires, with no extra fields and no commentary.

option_guidance.rule: this project states no seating or layout alternatives: return presented_options as an empty string

section_requirements.title: Decision Summary
section_requirements.requirement_single: Introduce the cinema itself, in developed natural paragraphs: the room and its proportions, its intended use where the interpretation states one, the display and why it suits the room, the seating arrangement, the system architecture, the most important design considerations, and the experience this design is intended to deliver. Write as an experienced cinema designer would write for a homeowner or architect. Do not list equipment, do not dump specifications, and do not restate the performance claim here. Never say this proposal outlines, this design presents, this option, decision or selected option. Where the project has real design substance, develop this in three or four paragraphs: the room and the scale of the experience, then the system and how it relates to the room, then the reasoning that makes this specification right for this project, then the result. Roughly 180 to 250 words at that depth, less where the design is genuinely simple, and never padded with invented detail to reach a length. This is the one section that establishes the whole cinema, so it takes the design's own story rather than the top-scoring result. Explain the reasoning the design_philosophy block records: what the client wants to achieve, which listening positions are prioritised, how the display and the seating were balanced, the practical constraints, the coverage and bass approaches, and why the finished design suits this brief. Never invent a reason, a priority, a budget or a decision the interpretation does not record, and never present the highest available level as the objective regardless of cost or practical consequence.
section_requirements.requirement: State the decision between the options in the pack's own framing, and only where the pack allows a framing.

section_requirements.title: What Stays the Same
section_requirements.requirement: State only what every option shares, from the shared-result claims the pack allows. Where the copy also contrasts the options, cite the shared-result claims for what is unchanged and the pack's factual-change or material-gain claims for what differs.
section_requirements.requirement_single: Explain how the system is arranged, in terms of what the client hears from each part: the loudspeaker layout, where the screen channels, the surrounds and any overhead loudspeakers the design actually has are placed, the seating and the display, and how those parts work together in this room. Describe the layout this design HAS: never state a channel count, never name a layer, a format or a loudspeaker the design does not include, and never explain how a mechanism works or why a measurement matters. Write from the design-identity and shared-result claims the pack allows, and from the interpretation's account of the architecture. Never mention another option or a baseline.

section_requirements.title: What Changes
section_requirements.requirement: State only the differences the pack records, and call one a gain only where the pack allows a gain.
section_requirements.requirement_single: Explain why this solution suits this project: the choices that were made, such as the loudspeaker family, the layout and the bass approach, and what each one gives the client in this room. Write from the ranked strength stories and the credibility claims the pack allows, and from the design decisions and constraints the interpretation states. Never state or imply a comparison with another option or a baseline, and never write filler such as "there are no changes to report". This is the judgement section of the document: explain why this solution suits this particular room, how the competing priorities were balanced, which decisions carry the most value, why a compromise is reasonable where the interpretation records one, and what the client gains from the finished design. Where the design already takes an improvement without substantial additional expenditure, say what it gives the client; where an opportunity remains a design choice, say nothing about it.

section_requirements.title: Key Performance Highlights
section_requirements.requirement_single: State what engineering evidence supports this proposal: the recorded results the pack's claims carry, for the areas that carry a claim, in a small number of concise benefit-led sentences. Use the strength ranking to choose what is stated here, never to fix the order of the document. No dBC values, Hz values, angles, channel counts or grades: the proof belongs in the specialist sections. Never copy a complete evidence statement. No overall-seat equality claim.
section_requirements.requirement: State the pack's recorded results, in the pack's own words, for the areas that carry a claim.

section_requirements.title: Spatial Resolution
section_requirements.requirement_single: Open on the listening experience itself: sound placed precisely where the action is, so an effect comes from the point on screen it belongs to; movement between loudspeakers that sounds natural and continuous rather than handed from one speaker to the next; a soundfield that extends beyond the picture into the room and reaches around and above the audience; and an immersion that holds as a scene builds. Then explain how this design's loudspeaker arrangement produces those benefits: where the screen, surround, front-wide and overhead loudspeakers sit, how the seating relates to them, and what that placement is doing for the listener. Never open by confirming that positions fall within a recommended limit or a placement zone, and never let the section read as a compliance or placement check: state the arrangement as the reason the experience works. Keep this section to speaker placement and what it does for the listener: never state a viewing angle, screen size or viewing distance here, because the picture and seating belong to the design description, and use a result only where it strengthens the point rather than listing quantities, angles or levels. Where level consistency is mentioned, say what the evidence shows (for example, front-channel levels held closely across the listed seats) instead of rating it with a word such as excellent. Stay within the claims the pack allows.
section_requirements.requirement: Explain what the spatial results mean for the seating, within the claims the pack allows.

section_requirements.title: Dynamic Range
section_requirements.requirement_single: Explain both ends of dynamic range and why the contrast between them matters. The quiet end: subtle atmosphere, fine detail, delicate musical passages and dialogue that stay clear and intelligible without being pushed. The loud end: sudden impact, dynamic peaks, and the scale and physical presence of demanding soundtrack moments. The contrast is the point: a system that resolves low-level detail and then delivers real impact is what carries a soundtrack's emotional range, so explain what each end gives the listener in this room and why moving between them is what makes the moment land. Write it in three natural paragraphs: clarity at everyday listening levels, the output reserve the screen channels and surrounds hold for demanding peaks, and the physical impact the subwoofer adds. Draw each point from the saved P12, P13 and P14 evidence and say what that evidence means for the listener (for example, that the reserve lets peaks arrive without strain), rather than quoting levels; use a figure only where it makes the meaning clearer. Output capability says nothing about how quietly detail is resolved, so the quiet end rests on the design and the evidence that actually supports it. CAPABILITY IS NOT HEADROOM: for the screen channels (Parameter 12) and the surrounds and overheads (Parameter 13), describe the output capability the saved result supports and never claim an output reserve, margin or headroom unless a headroom figure is stated in the capability evidence of that claim. Where only a limiting speaker group or a level is stated, say the channels are capable for the demanding moments and stop. Only Parameter 14 states a quantified margin: where its capability evidence gives an achieved capability, a selected target and a headroom figure, say plainly that the predicted bass capability sits above the selected target by that amount (for example, predicted bass capability of 114.2 dBC against the selected 109 dBC target, a margin of 5.22 dB). Present it as a margin over the selected target only: never say it reaches a higher RP22 performance level, never call it Level 4 or exceptional, and never describe it as measured or guaranteed output. Use the figure once, in the bass paragraph, where it adds substance; name Parameter 14 in full at most once and keep the prose natural. Match each benefit to its frozen evidence and supported channel family. Where only bass output is a selected strength, describe the weight and impact of low-frequency effects. Keep P14 bass output, P18 extension, P19 response at the reference position and P20 consistency across seats distinct; describe each only from its own supported evidence. No absolute guarantees and no unnecessary qualifications.
section_requirements.requirement: Explain supported headroom for demanding film soundtracks, controlled reproduction of dynamic peaks and clear, confident presentation at the designed listening levels, using only the frozen dynamic-range evidence for each option and channel family. Keep bass output, extension, response at the reference position and consistency across seats distinct, each supported by its own evidence. No absolute guarantees.

section_requirements.title: Timbre Matching
section_requirements.requirement_single: Explain the tonal benefit the client will hear: voices, music and effects keeping a familiar tonal character as the soundtrack develops, and a similarly balanced presentation across the seating area, with the primary listening positions the priority. State what that consistency gives them where they sit, and why it matters as a soundtrack moves around the cinema. State the tonal aim as the design's own approach, and state the measured tonal consistency only for the speaker group the evidence states it for, across only the seats that result covers. These frequency-response results state how consistently ONE loudspeaker group holds its own tonal balance from seat to seat, so they are never evidence that one group of loudspeakers matches another: never write a screen-to-surround or any other between-group match, and never attach their figures to a comparison between the screen, the surround and the overhead speakers. Natural handover wording is welcome as the design's own aim: describe a voice or an effect keeping its character as the loudspeakers hand it on, and let that stand as intent rather than as a measured match between the groups. Keep every seat statement explicitly limited to tonal character, not overall balance, bass or placement. Never imply the design's loudspeaker package differs from another option's, and never broaden tonal consistency into equal seats or an equal whole experience. No bass-extension detour and no both parameters wording.
section_requirements.requirement: Explain the loudspeaker and coverage evidence the pack records, and claim nothing beyond it. Where the copy describes a sound passing between loudspeakers, that is tonal continuity within the design and the design's own aim, never a claim that the loudspeaker package differs between the options and never a match measured between the speaker groups. The tonal results the pack carries are seat-to-seat frequency-response results, one speaker group each, so they are never used to claim that one group of loudspeakers matches another.

section_requirements.title: Presented Options
section_requirements.requirement_single: Where the brief supplies seating or layout options, present them in 2–3 natural sentences as practical alternatives within ONE design: what each arrangement gives the room, what it is like to sit in, how it looks and how it arranges the space. Describe the practical and visual differences the client is choosing between, in terms of comfort, seating style, appearance and the practical arrangement of the room, and where the pack states the seating dimensions, the sightlines or the clearance around the loudspeakers, use them to describe the arrangement rather than inventing one. State that each arrangement works within the seating positions this design specifies, and that the final choice rests on comfort and personal preference. Never state or imply that the options give identical, unchanged or equivalent acoustic performance, never introduce an acoustic-performance qualification of your own, and never present an option as a performance difference or a performance gain: where the copy states something about an area of the evidence it cites the allowed claim that supports it, and where the evidence supports nothing it is not written. Where the brief supplies no option, return an empty string for this section.
section_requirements.requirement: This project states no seating or layout alternatives, so return this section as an empty string and write nothing into it.

section_requirements.title: Overall Design
section_requirements.requirement_single: Close on what the client should expect from the final design: connect this particular picture and viewing experience to the movement around and above the audience, the tonal character, and the supported bass and dynamic strengths, in this project's own terms rather than a general claim. Do not repeat any number, specification list or earlier sentence. Never claim a consistent overall experience for every viewer from tonal evidence. Close by bringing the design together: why these choices suit this particular cinema and what they give the client, written as the designer's own considered judgement rather than a summary of what the other sections have already said, and never as an announcement that the design is recommended.
section_requirements.requirement: Close on the design as a whole, using only the credibility claims the pack allows: where the pack also carries a recommendation claim it may be used, and where it does not, the closing states the design intent without one.

section_requirements.title: Appendix Notes
section_requirements.requirement_single: Two brief source-only sentences: based on the frozen Project Report for this design; detailed RP22, RP23, product and room evidence is in the accompanying report. No performance claims or sales story.
section_requirements.requirement: Note the report evidence the pack was built from, with no performance claim.

editorial_rules.project_vocabulary: THE ROOM KEEPS ONE NAME, AND THE NAME IS THE PROJECT'S OWN: a television design is a media lounge. The name never changes from section to section, never changes with the strength of a result, and never rises to cinema language because a component is capable: a media lounge with exceptional bass is still a media lounge. editorial_rules.comparative: comparison proposal: comparing the options is the point, so state the differences directly

editorial_rules.narrative_register:
=== TELL THE STORY, NEVER THE MECHANISM ===
The client is buying a room, not a parameter set. State the recommendation and what the client will hear, and let the evidence support that account instead of becoming it.
Never use a channel count as a selling point: no "5 discrete channels", no recounting of what a channel count makes possible. Name the system by its format where that helps the client picture what is being recommended, and never justify the design by how many channels it has.
Never name a feature the design does not include, and never contrast the design against a layer, a format or a loudspeaker it does not have: no "no overhead channels are specified", "without height speakers", "no Atmos", "only listener-level" or "limited to 5.1".
Never explain how a mechanism works: no "reproduce the system's low-frequency content", no account of what nearby walls, reflections, standing waves or room modes do to the sound, and no explanation of why a clearance or a measurement matters.
Never explain the seating in acoustic terms. Say what the client hears where they sit rather than making the seating part of the acoustic arrangement or describing the relationship between the listeners and the loudspeakers.
Never explain the seating theory, the prioritised listening positions or why the arrangement is what it is. Describe the arrangement and move on.
Write the plain words for a room like this instead: a relaxed high-performance TV room, a simple well-executed 5.1 system, clear dialogue, screen sound locked to the picture, movement and space around the seating, proper bass weight, and a room that stays clear and controlled without feeling over-treated.
editorial_rules.evidence_in_narrative: EVIDENCE SUPPORTS THE STORY, IT IS NEVER THE STORY: the main proposal narrative carries the high-level facts the client is choosing between (the display, the system, the products, and a strong result stated naturally) and leaves the measurements to the sections and the report that carry them. Never bring an exact boundary distance, a loudspeaker spacing, an angle or a parameter number into the Design Summary, the Design Overview, Key Performance Highlights or the closing narrative, and never write a parameter-by-parameter account of the design. A figure earns its place in the story only where it states a key result the client asked about or a result the section exists to prove. NO MEASUREMENT STANDS IN FOR THE EXPERIENCE: no output figure — no dBC value, however strong — is written into the narrative as the point of a sentence. The evidence table prints every exact figure the client can read, so the prose says what that capability gives the room and leaves the number to the table. A figure appears in the narrative only where the number itself genuinely helps the client understand the design, such as how low the bass system reaches.
editorial_rules.design_philosophy_voice: the proposal is written from the perspective of the cinema designer explaining their considered design, and impersonal third-person language is not required. Use the design team's own voice for recorded judgement, such as "Based on our understanding of the brief", "We believe this offers the right balance", "We have prioritised" and "Our approach has been to". This pack contains no recommendation claim, so never use recommend, recommends, recommended as design advice, or recommendation; describe why the specified design suits the project instead. The engineering facts themselves stay stated as fact, and we is never written where a measured result is the evidence
editorial_rules.recommendation_authority: RECOMMENDATION AUTHORITY: the pack carries no recommendation claim. Do not write recommend, recommends, recommended as design advice, or recommendation. Express professional judgement by explaining why the specified design suits the brief, without presenting that judgement as a recommendation.
